strengths: Novel theoretical contributions: Theorem 3 provides a refined Lipschitz bound that explicitly captures attention distribution dependence via max_i||M(P^h_{i,:})||_2, improving over prior work (Theorems 1-2); Theorem 4 is a mathematically solid result on softmax Jacobian singular values using ordinal statistics

Practical approach that preserves dot-product attention: JaSMin is lightweight and integrates into standard training without architectural replacement, avoiding computational overhead and deployment complexity of prior methods
Solid technical soundness: Proofs are correct, the spectral norm decomposition in Theorem 3 is carefully done, and the interlacing theorem application in Theorem 4 is appropriate

Comprehensive experimental validation within scope: Consistent improvements over Specformer baseline on CIFAR-10/100 across FGSM, PGD, and AutoAttack; extensive hyperparameter sweeps (Tables 3-4); effective visualizations (Figures 2-6) demonstrate bound tightness and regularization effects

Valuable insights connecting attention distributions to Lipschitz constants: The observation that both uniform and concentrated distributions can yield small Lipschitz values is interesting for understanding transformer dynamics
weaknesses: Critical experimental limitation for a vision conference: Evaluation restricted to CIFAR-10/100 with no ImageNet validation (standard for ECCV vision transformer papers); only ViT-B architecture tested; no evaluation on language models or other domains mentioned in introduction—severely undermines generality claims

Theory-practice gap in regularization: Equation (3) specifies multiple components (||W^V_h||_2, ||P^h||_2, max_i||M(P^h_{i,:})||_2) but regularization (Equations 8-9) targets only one; Figure 6 shows JaSMin log₁₀ values ~2.0-2.5 vs. exact ~0.6-0.7, indicating the bound remains loose in practice

Unresolved theoretical contradiction: The paper claims both uniform AND categorical distributions yield small Lipschitz constants (Section 3, Figure 1), yet this is counterintuitive given the introduction's discussion of attention sinks as problematic; categorical distribution optimality lacks convincing justification

Modest practical improvements with accuracy trade-offs: Standard accuracy often drops (90.9%→89%, 98.56%→98.4%); AutoAttack improvements are small in absolute terms (~2% on best CIFAR-100 config); no systematic Pareto frontier analysis of robustness vs. accuracy trade-offs

Hyperparameter selection lacks principality: Optimal λ and k vary significantly across datasets and attacks (k∈{0,10,30}, λ∈{1e-2,1e-3,1e-4}); no principled selection criterion provided; introduces more hyperparameters than Specformer baseline

Missing ablation studies and analysis: No isolation of contributions from different regularization variants (mean vs. max, different k values); no computational overhead measurement despite lightweight claims; missing comparisons with recent robustness methods beyond Specformer; no certified defense baselines

Incomplete theoretical justification: Connection between local Lipschitz constants and practical adversarial robustness is theoretically motivated but not guaranteed; why constraining ordinal statistics leads to robustness remains unclear; Theorem 4's ordinal statistics feel somewhat disconnected from main bound application

strengths: Solid theoretical analysis with novel insights: Theorem 4 on softmax Jacobian interlacing properties is well-proven and provides a refined bound tighter than prior work; the connection between attention distributions (uniform vs. categorical) and Lipschitzness is insightful.

Tighter Lipschitz bounds than prior work: The refined bound in Theorem 3 accounts for attention distribution structure via max_i ||M(P^h_{i,:})||_2, shown empirically to be more accurate than Theorem 1 (Specformer) and competitive with Theorem 2.

Practical lightweight regularization: JaSMin is easy to implement without replacing dot-product attention; shows consistent improvements in adversarial robustness (FGSM, PGD, AutoAttack) across CIFAR-10/100 without major accuracy loss.

Clear presentation of core insights: Good intuitive explanations of how attention distributions affect robustness; effective visualizations (especially Figure 1 showing g_1 function and Figures 2-3 validating bound tightness).
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: Heavily builds on the Jacobian structure from prior work [18]; the improvement comes from accounting for softmax structure, which is relatively incremental. Theorem 4, while solid, applies classical interlacing theorem straightforwardly to softmax. The stronger O(√N) bound claimed in Appendix C should be the main result.

Severely limited experimental scope for a vision conference: Only CIFAR-10/100 validation is inadequate; no ImageNet or large-scale experiments despite discussing vision transformers. No language model experiments despite motivation extensively mentioning LLMs. Only ViT-B tested; missing ablations on other architectures.

Theory-practice gap inadequately addressed: The jump from bounding ||M(P^h_{i,:})||_2 to regularizing log g_1 lacks rigorous justification. Connection between local Lipschitz constants and adversarial robustness is assumed but not formally proven for this setting. Design choices (max vs. mean aggregation, choice of k in g_k regularization) are not systematically ablated.

Experimental validation concerns: Baseline appears undertrained (90.9% on CIFAR-100); extensive hyperparameter sweeps (Tables 3-4) show high variance with many configs worse than baseline; robustness improvements are modest; 'exact' Lipschitz constants computed via power iteration are not exact; missing comparisons to certified defense methods.

Incomplete technical comparison: Main paper reports Theorem 3 with O(N) dependence, while Appendix C hints at O(√N) improvements—this makes the main-text presentation misleading about improvements over Theorem 2. Detailed analysis of when Theorem 3 substantially outperforms Theorem 2 is deferred.

Missing critical ablation studies and analyses: No systematic ablation on max vs. mean aggregation in regularization; no ablation on k parameter; no analysis of whether Lipschitz reduction is the actual bottleneck for robustness; limited investigation of when attention naturally tends toward target distributions; no computational overhead analysis.

Presentation issues: Definition 1 labeling is confusing; Remark 1 on local bounds vague regarding neighborhood specification; ε ≈ 1e-6 hack to avoid division by zero (Appendix D) is inelegant; reproducibility concerns (no code, some implementation details missing like g_1 differentiation in backprop).

strengths: Novel refined Lipschitz bounds: Theorem 3 meaningfully tightens prior work by explicitly capturing attention distribution effects via M(P^h_{i,:}); Theorem 4 provides elegant ordinal statistics characterization of softmax Jacobian spectral norm

Strong theoretical insights: The observation that Lipschitz constants are small for uniform or categorical attention distributions provides valuable intuition about transformer stability and training preferences for larger sequences
Tight bounds in practice: Figures 2-3 demonstrate the bound g_1(P^h_{i,:}) closely approximates exact spectral norms across multiple heads and layers, validating theoretical tightness
Practical lightweight regularization: JaSMin is easy to integrate into existing pipelines without architectural modifications, unlike prior methods requiring attention mechanism replacement

Comprehensive experimental validation: Extensive hyperparameter sweeps (Tables 3-4), consistent improvements across multiple attack methods (FGSM/PGD/AutoAttack), good ablation studies, and informative visualizations of attention distributions
Sound technical execution: Proofs appear rigorous, proper handling of block matrix decomposition, and correct treatment of multi-head aggregation in theoretical analysis
weaknesses: Limited experimental scope: Evaluation restricted to CIFAR-10/100 and ViT-B; no ImageNet results despite ImageNet pretraining, no evaluation on larger models (ViT-L/H) or other architectures (RoBERTa, BERT), limiting generalizability claims

Modest practical improvements with accuracy-robustness trade-offs: Robustness gains often marginal (1-3% on FGSM4); some configurations suffer significant accuracy drops (90.9% → 88.85% standard accuracy); AutoAttack results mixed with baseline sometimes outperforming JaSMin variants

Incremental theoretical improvements: Appendix C reveals only constant-factor improvement over Theorem 2; the ||X||²_2||A_h||_2 term can still dominate the bound, limiting practical utility of the distribution-dependent refinement

Unclear causal link between bound reduction and robustness: Figure 4 shows correlational improvement in Lipschitz distributions but theoretical guarantee that minimizing the bound improves robustness is missing
Incomplete analysis of bound tightness: No characterization of when the bound becomes loose in practice, no analysis of failure modes or pathological cases where the bound provides little guidance

Experimental design limitations: Hyperparameter interaction effects not fully characterized (why different λ values for different k?), comparison with Specformer uses different hyperparameter ranges, missing reproducibility details (code availability, random seeds, exact computation procedures)
